source.title: Probing the Impact of Scale on Data-Efficient, Generalist Transformer World Models for Atari

page_placements.theme: Task diversity and context length affect generalization

record.tranche_reason: It sweeps transformer world-model capacity and reports validation-loss scaling behavior relevant to model-wise double descent, using Atari offline datasets and a validation-loss measure rather than reproducing the original experiments.
record.gate_note: The study reports validation-loss trends across model capacities, including individual and unified models and fixed-budget mixed-environment datasets. Downstream policy scores and reward-predictor results do not measure the claim’s scaling curves, so they are not rows. The paper cites prior work on double descent; cited results are not recorded as findings of this study.
record.test_reason: It sweeps transformer depth (L=2 to 96, about 6M to 300M parameters) for Atari world models on fixed 100k-transition offline datasets and reports validation loss against model size. This is a model-wise double-descent test in a new setting: generative world models and next-latent MSE rather than classification test error. It does not vary epochs or sample count, and it does not manipulate label noise or regularization.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that individual world models fall into task-dependent regimes: classical (bigger hurts), canonical double descent (Pong, Qbert), monotonic, and saturated. They find that unified training on 26 games makes scaling monotonic for all tasks, and that task diversity mitigates overfitting even at a fixed data budget (preliminary). They also find that properly scaled models support downstream policies at a median normalized score of 0.770. They read the classical regime as not yet past the interpolation threshold, despite near-zero training loss.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a transformer depth sweep on fixed offline Atari datasets and validation loss as the generalization measure. The study varies world-model settings and task mixtures rather than reproducing the original studies' experimental setups.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling behavior varies by environment and training setup; the Amidar overfitting spike is delayed more by mixing with Assault than by mixing with Gopher. Unified training is reported to stabilize the trends.

fits_no_version.finding: Joint training on 26 games, and to a lesser extent two-game mixtures under a fixed budget, removes or delays the inverted-U in validation loss versus model size. The authors frame this as task diversity acting as a regularizer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-task data diversity, at fixed or larger data volume, suppresses or shifts the model-wise overfitting peak.

record.problems: The central scaling results use validation loss rather than test error. Many trends are described qualitatively without exact loss values. The mixed-environment ablation is preliminary and restricted to two environment pairs. The study reports no direct manipulation of label noise or regularization.
record.rows_left_out: No further scaling outcomes left out. Downstream policy results and reward-predictor metrics were excluded because they do not measure the claim's scaling curves.

untested.parts: Width scaling for individual models; test error on supervised classification; label-noise settings; full-sweep shape without early stopping.
No epoch-wise analysis of test-loss shape.
Sample count is never varied; the mixture ablation holds total budget fixed.
Only transformer world models are tested.
No effective-complexity measure is computed. Task 'complexity' is a qualitative post-hoc explanation (Appendix D).
No label-noise manipulation, no multiple-descent test, and no regularization tuning. Weight decay is fixed at 0.1 and dropout at 0.

missing.what: Statement that the deepest models (L=96) reach near-zero training error across all environments. This is key evidence that interpolation is reached in classical-regime games without a second descent.
missing.locator: Section 4.2, final paragraph; Figure 2 bottom; Figure 12

missing.what: Training uses early stopping (patience 100 evaluations), and Figure 15 plots minimum validation loss under early stopping. Early stopping can suppress a double-descent peak, which affects reading every V1 row.

record.verdict_notes: Capacity is varied only by depth at d=512 for individual models; the unified sweep mixes depth and width. The measure is next-latent MSE validation loss with early stopping, not test error. The authors' Appendix D 'complexity' explanations are post hoc and qualitative. The V6 links in the record rested only on the authors' variance and noise interpretation, so they are removed. Downstream policy results are correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: Uses validation loss rather than test error. It does not show the full fall-rise-fall shape for every environment or establish that the peak is near an exact training-set interpolation size in every setting.
No epoch- or training-time sweep testing for a fall-rise-fall generalization curve.
No increase in the number of training samples near an interpolation threshold. The mixed-environment ablation holds the total data budget fixed.
Tests transformer world models, not a range of model classes or a general curve across model classes.
Does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
The authors attribute some overfitting behavior to variance, but do not manipulate label noise, test triple or multiple descent, or test whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
Does not re-express results using an effective parameter count to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: W_ind (Amidar)
rows.size_stated: approximately 6 million to 300 million parameters; fixed embedding dimension 512; L ∈ {2, 4, 8, 12, 24, 48, 96}
rows.operation_detail: Varied transformer depth for an individual Atari world model trained on a fixed offline dataset.

conditions.value: fixed offline dataset; 100k transitions per environment

rows.value: Training loss reaches zero for L ≥ 4; validation loss is lowest at L = 8 to L = 12 and degrades at L = 24, 48, and 96.
rows.uncertainty: One standard error; curves averaged over eight independent runs.
rows.note: The authors describe this as a classical U-shaped validation-loss curve and say the interpolation threshold has not been surpassed.
rows.check: State 'reversed' is wrong. The first fall and the rise do appear (best at L=8-12, worse at L=24-96). But the paper says training loss is near zero for L≥4, yet there is no second descent up to L=96. The final descent V1 predicts past the interpolating size is absent. The authors' claim that the threshold 'has not been surpassed' conflicts with V1's training-fit definition. Remove the V6 link: no noise or regularization is manipulated, and the variance attribution is interpretation.

rows.subject: W_ind (Assault)
rows.size_stated: approximately 6 million to 300 million parameters; fixed embedding dimension 512; L ∈ {2, 4, 8, 12, 24, 48, 96}
rows.operation_detail: Varied transformer depth for an individual Atari world model trained on a fixed offline dataset.

conditions.value: fixed offline dataset; 100k transitions per environment

rows.value: Validation performance improves monotonically as model depth increases; the authors state even the smallest models in the sweep are beyond the interpolation threshold.
rows.uncertainty: One standard error; curves averaged over eight independent runs.
rows.note: Reports a monotonic post-threshold trend, not the full fall-rise-fall curve.
rows.check: Monotonic improvement with no peak in the sweep. This is consistent only with the post-threshold side of V1, and the authors assert rather than show that the threshold lies below L=2.

rows.subject: W_ind (Freeway)
rows.size_stated: approximately 6 million to 300 million parameters; fixed embedding dimension 512; L ∈ {2, 4, 8, 12, 24, 48, 96}
rows.operation_detail: Varied transformer depth for an individual Atari world model trained on a fixed offline dataset.

conditions.value: fixed offline dataset; 100k transitions per environment

rows.value: Curves for L = 8 through L = 96 essentially overlap; the authors say saturation occurs at L = 4.
rows.uncertainty: One standard error; curves averaged over eight independent runs.
rows.note: The authors report no significant further gain after early saturation.
rows.check: Curves are flat from L=4 or L=8 onward. No peak or second descent appears in the sweep.

rows.subject: W_ind (Pong)
rows.size_stated: approximately 6 million to 300 million parameters; fixed embedding dimension 512; L ∈ {2, 4, 8, 12, 24, 48, 96}
rows.operation_detail: Varied transformer depth for an individual Atari world model trained on a fixed offline dataset.

conditions.value: fixed offline dataset; 100k transitions per environment

rows.value: Validation loss improves from L = 2 to L = 8, worsens from L = 12 to L = 48, and declines again at L = 96, eventually surpassing the L = 8 result.
rows.uncertainty: One standard error; curves averaged over eight independent runs.
rows.note: The authors call this the canonical double-descent trajectory and attribute the intermediate deterioration to fitting training noise before the final descent.
rows.check: Remove the V6 link. The 'fitting training noise' explanation is the authors' interpretation, not a noise manipulation.

rows.subject: Aggregate of individual world models in the classical regime: Alien, Amidar, Breakout, Gopher, Kangaroo, MsPacman
rows.operation_detail: Categorized individual-model validation-loss curves by their trend over the depth sweep.
rows.note: This is the paper's reported aggregate classification; the six environments are listed in the subject.
rows.check: State 'reversed' is wrong. Per Section 4.2, the deepest models reach near-zero training error in all environments, yet larger models keep hurting with no second descent. Remove the V6 link. This is a categorization from curves with no numbers given.

rows.subject: Aggregate of individual world models in the canonical regime: Pong, Qbert
rows.operation_detail: Categorized individual-model validation-loss curves by their trend over the depth sweep.
rows.value: Count 2; categorized as “Bigger hurts, then helps.”
rows.note: The text describes the full trajectory for Pong; Table 1 assigns both Pong and Qbert to this regime.
rows.check: Remove the V6 link. Only Pong's trajectory is described in the text; Qbert's classification rests on Figure 12.

rows.subject: Aggregate of individual world models in the monotonic regime: Assault, Asterix, Boxing, ChopperCommand, CrazyClimber, DemonAttack, Hero, Jamesbond, Krull, PrivateEye, RoadRunner, UpNDown
rows.operation_detail: Categorized individual-model validation-loss curves by their trend over the depth sweep.
rows.note: The stated monotonic improvement is a regime classification, not evidence of the full double-descent trajectory within each environment.
rows.check: No peak observed; monotonic improvement only. This is a regime classification.

rows.subject: Aggregate of individual world models in the saturated regime: BankHeist, Battlezone, Freeway, Frostbite, KungFuMaster, Seaquest
rows.operation_detail: Categorized individual-model validation-loss curves by their trend over the depth sweep.
rows.value: Count 6; categorized as “Small is already big.”
rows.note: This is the paper's reported aggregate classification; the six environments are listed in the subject.
rows.check: No peak and no change beyond small depths; regime classification only.

rows.subject: Aggregate of 26 separately trained individual Atari world models
rows.operation_detail: Reported the average validation-loss trend across the 26 individual world models.
rows.value: The global average improves monotonically with depth through L = 48; the paper attributes this to the 12/26 tasks in the monotonic regime.
rows.uncertainty: One standard error; curves averaged over eight independent runs.
rows.note: The aggregate trend does not show the full fall-rise-fall shape.
rows.check: This aggregate averages over four regimes, so it cannot show a per-task shape. The authors say it holds 'up to L = 48'.

rows.subject: W_uni (single unified world model trained on all 26 Atari environments)
rows.size_stated: Under-parameterized baselines: L = 8, d ∈ {512, 1024}; over-parameterized configurations: L ∈ {4, 8, 24}, d = 2048; largest approximately 1.2 billion parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation-loss trends across unified-model configurations of differing capacity.

conditions.value: aggregated fixed offline datasets from all 26 Atari environments
all 26; the paper reports improvement or stabilization across tasks

rows.value: Once in the over-parameterized regime, larger models consistently improve or sustain performance; the paper reports no rank reversals or inverted-U curves.
rows.note: The reported configurations differ in both depth and embedding dimension. The paper says the solid-line configurations reach near-zero training loss.
rows.check: Only five configurations are tested, varying depth and width jointly. Loss falls monotonically from the under-parameterized to the over-parameterized models with no peak or inverted-U (Figure 13). The size axis is coarse.
